name: Diego Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm the lead carpenter for Hollins Homes, a small builder that does about twenty houses a year on plots around town. I run the carpentry from floor joists to roof, and I'm the one the site manager phones when the drawings don't add up. Weekends I've got my own little business, building decks and garden rooms, which is where my heart is. What wears me out is working six days, and what I love is a Sunday afternoon at church with nothing to build.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. For the deck business I describe the garden, and the AI draws three designs and a price, and customers love seeing it before they pay. At Hollins I use it to check spans and work out the order for materials. I even had it write the words for my van, Reyes Decks and Garden Rooms, built right the first time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Marisol works part-time at the pharmacy, and we've got Mateo, twelve, and Sofia, eight. Mortgage on a three-bed near the park. Savings are thin, under a month, because every spare bit went into tools and a trailer for the weekend business, and Hollins pays less than the city firms, but the city's ninety minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. At work I'd tell the lads to use it anyway, it saves time. Online I'd keep posting my decks, the AI drawings bring in more customers than anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. My plan was always to grow the deck business until I can leave Hollins, and AI being just a good tool doesn't change that. It's a bit slower than I hoped, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep both jobs going and keep using the AI for designs and quotes. I'd try to book two decks a month instead of one this coming spring. I'd put the extra into paying down the trailer loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two jobs, six days a week. What does Marisol think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm mad, and she's right. But she also likes the extra money when the car needs tyres. Our deal is no work on Sunday, and the day I break that she's allowed to sell the trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do you think you could leave Hollins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If spring goes well, maybe in three years. I'd need four or five months saved first, which we're nowhere near. I won't gamble the house on it, the family comes first.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and tell the crew to use it anyway. I'd keep posting AI-drawn deck designs online because they bring in customers.
S0.think: I think it suits me, because my plan is to grow my deck business until I can leave Hollins. AI staying a good tool just makes that a bit slower.
S0.do: Keeps both jobs and uses AI daily for designs and quotes. Aims for two decks a month next spring and uses the extra to pay down the trailer loan.
S0.quote: Our deal is no work on Sunday, and the day I break that she's allowed to sell the trailer.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is an entrepreneur at heart who uses AI as a sales tool for his weekend business. The plateau doesn't touch his plan. His family comes first: a Sunday rule and a refusal to gamble the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work and learn. At work I'd tell the lads to get ahead of it. Online I'd show how I use the tools for my business, because people ask me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. If the design and paperwork side gets easier, a small business like mine can compete with the big boys. Hollins might need fewer carpenters, but I'd be the last one they let go, and by then I might not need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into renting one of those small cutting robots for the deck business, so I can cut a whole deck in a morning in the yard. I'd keep learning every AI tool that helps with quoting and design. I'd push to move to four days at Hollins and three on my own work once the bookings are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit like the start of spring, lots to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would worry about robots in this picture. Why don't you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather own the robot than compete with it. If a machine can cut my joists in half the time, that's two more decks a month, and two more decks is Mateo's football boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hollins would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek, the oldest of our framers. He's solid, but he doesn't like anything with a screen. I'd tell him to come and work weekends with me, learn it slowly, no pressure.

S1.say: I'd say steady change is a chance for anyone willing to work and learn. I'd tell colleagues to get ahead of it and show online how I use the tools.
S1.think: I think it's good for me because easier design and paperwork let small firms like mine compete with big ones. Hollins might cut carpenters, but I'd be last to go and might not need them by then.
S1.do: Looks into renting a small cutting robot for the deck business and keeps learning AI tools for quoting. Pushes to cut to four days at Hollins once bookings allow.
S1.feel: Positive, like the start of a busy spring.
S1.quote: If a machine can cut my joists in half the time, that's two more decks a month, and two more decks is Mateo's football boots.
S1.fieldNote: Diego sees steady disruption as an opening for small business, which fits his free-market outlook and appetite for risk. He'd rather own the machine than compete with it. He offers a struggling colleague a place on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and adapt fast, and waiting for the government won't help. At church I'd say look after each other. Online I'd share what I'm doing, so others can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years worries me. I like change, but I need money to ride it, and I've got less than a month of it. If AGI can design and build a deck by 2028, my little business is up against firms with robot crews and deep pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back at home, no holiday, no new van, and I'd go hard on the deck business to get as many jobs in as I could before it all shifts. I'd rent a robot as soon as one's available and pitch myself as the local man with a machine, faster and cheaper than Hollins. If Hollins cut me, I'd go full time on my own and make it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but switched on. Like the first winter I went self-employed on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms with deep pockets. How does a man with one trailer compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being local and being someone people know from church and the school gate. The big firm has the robots, but I'm the one who'll come back on a Sunday night when the gate won't shut. Well, Monday night. Marisol's rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident. What would keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, if two bad months came together. I'd be juggling, and I hate owing. If it went badly, I'd ask my brother for a loan before I'd ask any office for help.

S2.say: I'd say people need to adapt fast and stand on their own feet rather than wait for government. I'd share online what I'm doing so others can copy it.
S2.think: I think two years worries me because I need money to ride change and have under a month saved. My business would be up against firms with robot crews and deep pockets.
S2.do: Cuts holidays and a planned van at home and pushes hard to book deck jobs quickly. Rents a robot as soon as possible to compete locally and goes full time on his own if Hollins lets him go.
S2.feel: Nervous but switched on, like his first winter running a weekend business.
S2.quote: The big firm has the robots, but I'm the one who'll come back on a Sunday night when the gate won't shut.
S2.fieldNote: Diego's adaptability gives him a plan even in the fastest picture, but his thin cushion makes him nervous. He leans on being local and known, and would turn to his brother before any government help. He keeps his family's Sunday rule even in his own answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and anyone with sense will get ready. At work I'd tell the younger lads to learn to run the machines, not fight them. I'd keep posting my jobs online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is close to perfect for my plan. It's long enough to build the deck business, save some months, and buy a robot of my own before the big firms flood in. After 2031, I don't know what happens, honestly, but I'd rather be the owner than the worker when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd book every deck and garden room I can and save hard, aiming for three months in the bank. By year two or three I'd buy a second-hand cutting robot, even with a small loan, and leave Hollins once the business pays the mortgage. I'd train Mateo on Saturdays if he's interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a good kind. More excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a loan for a robot. Isn't that a risk with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd only do it once I had three months saved. I've seen men go under borrowing for the shiny thing. I'll take a risk with my own back, but not with Sofia's bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if after 2031 the robots don't need an owner like you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I hope I'd have something to sell, a name, a customer list, a machine. That's the point of building a business. A wage stops when the job stops; a business can be sold.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and sensible people will get ready. I'd tell young workers to learn to run machines rather than fight them.
S3.think: I think five years nearly fits my plan: build the business, save a few months and buy a robot before big firms arrive. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd rather be the owner than the worker.
S3.do: Books every job he can and saves towards three months of cushion. Buys a second-hand cutting robot by year two or three, possibly with a small loan, and leaves Hollins once the business covers the mortgage.
S3.feel: More excited than scared, a good kind of uneasy.
S3.quote: I'll take a risk with my own back, but not with Sofia's bedroom.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Diego's ideal window to move from worker to owner. He sets himself a clear line, three months saved, before borrowing. His thinking is classically free-market: a business can be sold when a wage cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd tell the lads at Hollins to start something on the side now. At church I'd say teach the kids to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years worries me a little, because it's long enough for everyone else to catch up. My edge right now is that I'm early. In ten years every builder has a robot, and then what makes me different?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the deck business steadily, leave Hollins in about three years, and buy my own machines by year five. I'd look at a second line, maybe maintaining and fixing building robots for other small firms, because someone has to. I'd save for the kids' futures properly for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Hopeful, but I'd keep looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Mateo and Sofia in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo likes building, he helps me on Saturdays. I'd want him to learn the trade and the machines both. A boy who can frame a wall and fix the robot that frames it won't go hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep looking over your shoulder. What are you watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms getting so cheap that small men like me can't compete. That's how markets work, and I won't moan about it. I'd just want to have sold up before that day, not after.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd tell colleagues to start a side business now and tell parents at church to teach children to be useful.
S4.think: I think ten years worries me a little because everyone catches up and I lose my early edge. When every builder has a robot, I'm not sure what makes me different.
S4.do: Grows the deck business, leaves Hollins in about three years and buys his own machines by year five. Adds robot repair for small firms and saves properly for his children.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, while watching over his shoulder.
S4.quote: A boy who can frame a wall and fix the robot that frames it won't go hungry.
S4.fieldNote: Oddly, the slowest picture is not Diego's favourite: it erodes his early-mover advantage. He accepts market competition without complaint and plans to sell before it squeezes him. He wants his son to learn both hand skills and machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have the ideas but not the money to ride it. What would help is small business loans you can get without a pile of paperwork, and apprenticeships that teach the machines, not just the hand tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about men like Derek. I'll be fine because I'm hungry for it, but not everyone's built that way, and they're not lazy, they're just good at what they did.

headlineQuote: I'll be fine because I'm hungry for it, but not everyone's built that way, and they're not lazy, they're just good at what they did.
portrait: Diego Reyes is a 43-year-old lead carpenter for a small home builder who runs a weekend deck and garden room business, with two kids, a wife at a pharmacy, a mortgage and under a month saved because his spare money went into tools. He uses AI daily for designs and quotes and sees new technology as a chance to become his own boss. He's calm about the plateau and steady disruption, and anxious but busy when AGI comes in two years. Five years is his ideal window to save, buy a robot and leave his employer. Ten years worries him a little because everyone else would catch up.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have plans but not the money to ride out the change.
whatWouldHelp: Small business loans without heavy paperwork, and apprenticeships that teach machines as well as hand tools.
